sourceFacts: A childhood upper respiratory infection can impair Eustachian tube ventilation and drainage, allowing middle-ear fluid to accumulate.
Fluid can persist after acute otitis media; effusion alone does not prove ongoing acute infection.
prompt:
Create an entirely original medical teaching concept illustration, landscape 3:2, warm hand-painted watercolour and gouache on ivory paper, fine ink contours, restrained navy labels, muted teal, ochre and peach accents, generous whitespace. Gentle storybook warmth with the precision and legibility of an educational atlas. Use written instructions only; no image reference. Meaningful visual relationships and sparse short labels, not paragraphs in boxes. NO internal anatomy, organ/eye/ear/brain/tissue cutaways, anatomical pathways, bones, diagnostic images, fake scans, realistic lesions, photorealistic skin, glossy wet flesh or 3D tissue. Neutral symbols or fully clothed surface poses only where specified. Preserve every direction, relationship and count in the explicit structure. Title and labels exactly as requested, no additional prose. Footer 'Educational schematic'. No logo or watermark.

Title 'After a respiratory infection'. Use a three-stage left-to-right visual mechanism built from abstract objects, explicitly no ears, head, throat or bodily tube. Left: a small folded tissue and a round spiked respiratory-virus SYMBOL, labelled 'Respiratory infection'. Middle: two small abstract flow ribbons, one air swirl and one water drop, each narrowed by a simple gate icon; labels 'Less ventilation' and 'Less drainage'. Both ribbons feed the RIGHT stage, a shallow open glass bowl with pooled blue drops labelled 'Fluid can remain'. Beneath the bowl a small calendar with fading ochre symptom marks is labelled 'Acute symptoms may settle first'. Direction arrows all left-to-right. Draw no microbes within fluid and do not equate every effusion with active infection. All objects are visual metaphors, not a substitute anatomical pathway. NO snowflakes, wind, temperature symbols or cold-weather cues. Infection is the initiating concept; the virus icon is generic, not microbiological anatomy.
